opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of it comes down to where the decisions are actually being made. When I was doing governance research in academia, at the Centre for the Governance of AI, I came to believe that many of the most consequential choices about how advanced AI gets developed and deployed would be made inside a handful of frontier labs, often under time pressure and with a lot of technical detail that's hard to see from outside. Academic work matters a great deal for shaping the broader conversation, but there's often a long, lossy chain between a paper and an actual decision.

Being inside DeepMind shortens that chain considerably. You're in the room, or near it, when questions come up about what safety evaluations a model should go through before release, what commitments the company should make, how to engage with governments, or how to think about things like access to model weights. And you can bring a governance perspective early, when it's still cheap to change course, rather than critiquing after the fact.

There's also an information advantage that runs both ways. Inside, you develop a much more grounded sense of what the technology can actually do, where it's heading, and what's realistically feasible to implement, which I think makes the policy thinking better. And you can help translate between technical researchers and leadership on one side, and policymakers and the broader public on the other.

I'd add that DeepMind in particular had, from its founding, a leadership that took the long-term risks and benefits of AI seriously, so there was real receptivity to this kind of advice. That matters a lot. Advising is only impactful if people want to listen, and I felt there was a genuine opportunity to help an important institution get some of these really high-stakes questions right.

Of course, there are trade-offs. You give up some independence, and you have to be thoughtful about that. But on balance, given how much leverage these labs have over the trajectory of the technology, it seemed like one of the highest-impact places I could be.

r001.rationale: The response says being inside DeepMind gives the adviser a grounded view of the technology and feasibility, and puts them near leaders as consequential decisions arise.

r002.rationale: It describes advising DeepMind leaders on company decisions and translating between technical researchers, leadership, and policymakers, indicating access to multiple decision makers.

r003.rationale: The response discusses high stakes and institutional leverage but does not argue that outcomes at pivotal historical moments can depend heavily on particular individuals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'd spent a long time at the Centre for the Governance of AI, and later at the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford, thinking about AI governance from the outside — building the field, writing research agendas, trying to map out what the big questions were. And I think that work was really valuable, and it still is. But over time I came to feel that a lot of the most consequential decisions about how this technology gets developed and deployed are being made inside a small number of frontier labs, and that the research we were doing on the outside only mattered to the extent that it actually changed what those organisations did.

So there's a kind of transmission problem. You can write a great paper on, say, compute governance or structured access or how to think about race dynamics, and it gets read by people in policy and academia, but whether it actually shapes the choices of the people deciding what to build, how to evaluate it, and when to release it — that's a much less certain path. Being inside means you're in the room when those decisions are being framed, and often the biggest leverage isn't in the final decision but in how the question gets posed in the first place.

The other thing is just information. From the outside, you're working with a fairly impoverished picture of what the frontier actually looks like — what's technically feasible, what the real bottlenecks are, what the internal culture and incentives are. A lot of governance thinking suffers from being either too abstract or being calibrated to a version of the technology that's a few years out of date. Inside, you get to ground your work in what's really happening, and that makes the advice much more useful and, frankly, much more likely to be taken seriously.

And then there's a more specific reason with DeepMind, which is that it's an organisation whose leadership has, since the beginning, taken these long-term questions seriously. Demis and Shane have been thinking about AGI and its risks for a long time. So it wasn't a case of going in and trying to convince people from scratch that any of this matters. It was more that there was genuine appetite for rigorous thinking about governance, and a gap in terms of having people whose full-time job was to do that thinking and connect it to the technical and strategic choices being made.

I should say, I don't think inside is strictly better than outside. There are real costs: you lose some independence, you can't say everything you'd want to say publicly, and there's always the risk that you end up being co-opted or just rationalising what the organisation was going to do anyway. I try to stay quite alert to that. But my judgement was that on the margin, given how much of the action was concentrated in a few places, having people with a governance and safety mindset embedded there — and still connected to the broader research and policy community — was one of the highest-leverage things I could do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says being inside puts the adviser in the room as decisions are framed and provides a clearer view of technical realities, internal culture, and incentives.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts the uncertain path from outside research to lab choices with being inside and able to connect advice to the people making those choices.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses concentrated decision-making and names DeepMind leaders, but does not argue that outcomes at pivotal historical moments depend heavily on particular individuals.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic intuition was that, if you want to help society navigate the development of very powerful AI, it’s valuable to be close to the place where that technology is being developed. There are important decisions about what to build, how to evaluate it, when to deploy it, and what safeguards you need. Being inside an organisation gives you an opportunity to inform those decisions while they’re still being shaped.

There’s also an information advantage. From the outside, you can do valuable work on governance, but you’re often reasoning with a fairly abstract picture of the technology and the choices available. Inside, you can talk to researchers, understand the constraints they face, and get a better sense of which governance proposals could actually work. That can make your advice much more useful.

And then there’s the question of whether the organisation is receptive. The opportunity is especially promising when people making consequential decisions take the risks seriously and want help thinking them through. Proximity alone doesn’t give you impact; you need a route from your analysis to a better decision.

So that was the attraction: combining work on the broader governance problem with an opportunity to make it concrete at one of the organisations developing the technology.

r001.rationale: The response says that being inside lets an adviser understand the technology, constraints, and choices facing the organization, making advice more useful.

r002.rationale: It says proximity creates an opportunity to inform decisions, but does not explain that working inside expands the set of decision makers the adviser can influence.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that outcomes at pivotal historical moments can depend heavily on particular individuals.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic thought was that a lot of consequential decisions about AI would be made within the organisations developing it. Governments have a crucial role, of course, but the people building these systems also make choices about what to develop, how to assess the risks, and when and under what conditions to deploy them.

Being inside an organisation gives you a better opportunity to understand those choices and make advice useful. You can learn what the technical constraints are, what decisions are actually coming up, and where there’s room to do things differently. And you can have an ongoing conversation with decision makers, rather than just publishing something and hoping it reaches them.

So the attraction was the possibility of bringing a governance perspective into those decisions early enough to matter. That doesn’t mean any particular piece of advice will be decisive. But if the decisions are sufficiently consequential, helping improve even a few of them could be very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says being inside helps an adviser learn the technical constraints and understand which decisions are coming up.

r002.rationale: It describes ongoing conversations with decision makers, but does not clearly say that being inside expands the set of decision makers the adviser can influence.
